utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning. Judge Nosworthy is sitting in the Martic trial. We're satisfied that it's in the interests of justice to continue in her absence today, so we will be sitting as a Bench of three this morning. Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. Your evidence will now continue. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I proceed, may I just take the opportunity of introducing to the Court and to the parties Mr. Keith Scully, who is sitting to my right. I should have done that yesterday, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. When we broke off last we were discussing the method of research for the preparation of the different parts of the report As Seen, As Told -- Under Orders. And you had discussed the first section of the book which you described as the background and historical section of the book. The staff involved in that, in the preparation of that part of the book, did they have any special skills in regard to the background and the history that they wrote about?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Researchers in the organisation are specialised in the countries that they cover. They often know the languages, are familiar with the history and the politics, and, most importantly, they undertake what we call missions to the field, in other words, fact-finding trips to investigate the situation on the ground. So this was the case for all of the reports that Human Rights Watch produced in relation to Kosovo and with regards to this background section in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you say the second part of the report focussed on the period from February 1998 until the commencement of the NATO bombing in March 1999. Can you again describe the method of research to gather the material for that part.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary source of information for all of our reports and this section in particular is the -- the field missions, the investigative trips. Between the period of February 1998 and March 1999, we conducted four separate research missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into Kosovo -- in Kosovo, to interview the witnesses and victims of abuses, to meet with lawyers and also obtain information from government sources, when possible. So this section of the report is the result of those efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you tell us about the research methodology in respect to the third section, which deals with the period of the NATO bombing from March to June 1999.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia commenced, we deployed researchers to the borders and had someone on the ground in Kosovo and Macedonia -- excuse me, in Albania and Macedonia throughout the period of the air campaign. These individuals were Human Rights Watch researchers who had experience, both -- most of them in the Balkans, but all of them in -- at least in other places if not the Balkans, in conducting human rights investigations. Their main task was to interview the individuals who were leaving Kosovo, to obtain information from them about the situation inside Kosovo. The main source -- the main technique is the one-on-one interview, which is standard procedure for the organisation. These are done in quiet settings whenever possible. There were times when these interviews in a few cases were quick because somebody was literally coming across the border in their tractor and we only had time to ask: Where are you from and why are you leaving? But the vast majority of these interviews were done in a private and quiet setting. They last sometimes many hours, sometimes more than one session, to obtain detailed information. We do not use questionnaires. We conduct interviews in an open format, an open narrative format, that allow the witness to speak about what they want to speak about. We refrain from asking leading questions. And we probe, very deeply, what I would call a -- a cynical understanding. We try to be sympathetic but also doubt every piece of information that is given to us so that we can confirm it, either through that interview or other interviews or other investigative means. So the results of those interviews are what we produced in the flashes that you mentioned yesterday, and they also form the basis for the section of the report in Under Orders that you are referring to now. I would only add that we supplemented that material after June 12th when we entered Kosovo. We had an individual -- a researcher in the province from June 14th, if I'm not mistaken, and we maintained a presence in Kosovo until -- for the next six months, very often more than one person. I went two, possibly three, times in the second half of 1999. And we attempted to visit the places that we had heard about from refugees during the NATO bombing. So we visited the villages in which these individuals had told us that crimes had occurred. And I -- as I have written in the report and I will state it today, I was surprised by the level of consistency in their testimonies. In other words, the details that refugees gave us during the bombing to a great extent matched with what we found on the ground. Names and places that were told to us, we were able to confirm from other interviewees or our visits to the specific sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. About how many interviewers did you have in that period from March to June when you were gathering the information for that part of the report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the borders, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that -- I would have to consult the report to be sure, but it was definitely at least six -- at different times. Not all at the same time, a rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And again, where your statement indicates that you participated as well --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- in those interviews, about how many persons were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you how many people were interviewed only in the period March to June. I could obtain that information if it's of interest to the Court. But I do know that from the period March 1999 through December 1999 we interviewed more than 600 different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I take it from that that there were more than 600 different interviews or 600 persons were interviewed for the purposes of the report in respect to that period, the period March to June?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, briefly, you said earlier that the methodology in writing the report itself now was the same in respect to all the sections. Can you tell us a little bit about that methodology in writing the report, and I would like you to focus also on quality-control procedures.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report -- the -- I was the primary author of the report and I wrote a per cent -- a large percentage of the chapters, but some of my colleagues also -- they wrote the sections that they in particular researched. So I would have to go through the report to tell you exactly which ones I wrote based on my personal research versus what they wrote based on theirs. However, in all cases the -- I edited and reviewed the sections that they wrote, and in most cases they edited and reviewed the sections I wrote. At the same time, all of our reports go through a rigorous editing process. In this case, with Under Orders, everything was reviewed by one outside reviewer, by our programme office and, thirdly, by our counsel's office, our legal office. In addition, the chapter on statistical analysis had a professional review by three statisticians, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to ask you about the statistical section. Who are the three statisticians; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The primary collaboration was with Dr. Patrick Ball, which -- who is from the American Association for the Advancement of Science, AAAS. And we had cooperation then from -- actually, three other statisticians, so four in total. We worked with Dr. Herb Spirer, who was teaching at Columbia University, and we had a professional review by two outside statisticians, Dr. Ray Smith, and -- I apologise, but I am now forgetting the name of the fourth. I could refer to the report if --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's in the report?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lastly, in respect to the report, what criteria, if any, was used in selecting the persons to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We chose individuals who we thought had stories to tell. Either we discovered them through our own canvassing or they were referred to us, for example, by journalists or by -- by other Albanians, humanitarian aid workers who said: Here's a person I think you should interview. So we would sit down this those people. And it is true, and we mentioned this in the chapter on statistical analysis, that our data cannot be extrapolated to all of Kosovo because we did seek out individuals whom we thought had knowledge of crimes. So we are very clear on the limitations of the data in that sense to make sure nobody makes conclusions beyond what the data speaks to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the purposes of this case, the -- the report discusses events in the Drenica region, the Djakovica region, the Istok region, the Orahovac region, the Pec region, the Prizren region, the Djakovica region, and the Suva Reka region, and the Vucitrn region. Can you comment briefly on -- or summarise the reports that you received in respect to the exodus of people from those regions.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of interviewees told us that they had been forcibly expelled from their villages, towns, or cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, again -- excuse me. We're getting into conclusions now. He's testifying to conclusions from the data that was amassed, and I would object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think, Mr. Sepenuk, we are being told not what the conclusion is but what the overwhelming majority of interviewees said. And I think that is admissible in the context in which we have reserved, until we've heard this evidence, the question of admissibility. And therefore, I will repel your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, you're telling us the reasons they told you for their departure, and it was that they were expelled from their villages, towns, or cities. Did they tell you by who?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many of the villagers could not identify the specific forces, whether the special police, the police, in a detailed manner, but they were very clear that it was government forces, either Serbian police, Yugoslav army, or, in some cases, local militias or paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll follow the order of the indictment for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The first point I'd like to ask you about is something you just mentioned a few moments ago, where you said that between March and June, when you were -- had your people in Albania and Macedonia, six people at different times, you interviewed people. Then you added that between March and December, going beyond June to December, is when you amassed the vast majority of your interviews, the 600.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you now exactly how many were done in the first period versus the second. That information can be obtained if it's of interest to you, but I'm not sure that the latter part was the majority. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If something like this arises that probably isn't controversial but is material that you feel it would be useful to have, then arrangements can be made for communication after the witness has concluded his evidence. I'm happy for you to relay to court staff something that you think ought to be obtained from a witness and try to make arrangements informally or try to ask the Bench to arrange it if you feel that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, would you have that information?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The database we compiled in preparation of the chapter on statistics is public. We have left it as an open source so others may utilise it, and that database would record the date and place of interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, how many interviewers did you have between June and December 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll give me a moment to recall. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My point is this: You only had six people, you said, on a rotating basis during the NATO campaign.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you continued interviews between June and December. Did you have many more people in that latter period?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. We definitely had -- I'm aware right now of five individuals. There may have been more, but there were at least that, again not all at the same time, but coming in and out. And we had at least one person at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Under Orders, which is for the record P438, we've seen and we've heard that it was published in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know which month it was published in 2001?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was October.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you've just finished telling us that you have direct involvement, both as an author and as an editor and the project manager, I think, or overseer of that publication. Is that fair and correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. So the work in drafting Under Orders, would that have taken place in the first half of 2001 and the latter part of 2000? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were employed by the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in -- for periods of 2000 and 2001, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was here April, May, and June of two thousand and -- of 2000 and in August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One of your tasks, I believe, was to collect materials for the Office of the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were also -- another one of your tasks in that period was that you were an investigator for the OTP, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My title was research analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you were also an investigator, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- my tasks were to do analysis and collect documents, but the investigators were doing more of the -- of the crime scene analysis, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So is it your position that you were not an investigator with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is I was a research analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. In 2001 you interviewed a man named Batan Haxhiu; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And for the record, this Albanian surname in English is spelled H-a-x-h-i-u. Now, Mr. Haxhiu was a journalist; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he gave a written statement which he signed and which you signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that was an ICTY witness statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haxhiu testified in the Milosevic trial on the 23rd of May, 2002, at page 5385, and he was asked this question. Mr. Haxhiu was asked: "You spoke to an investigator, whose name is Fred Abrahams. Is that correct? "A. Yes, yes, apart from him there was also someone else present at the meeting." Then the accused said: "I did not" -- says to the Judge: "I did not ask him about the presence of others but only about Fred Abrahams. His answer is yes, so can I move on?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY SAYS
utterances.text: "Yes. Bear that in mind, if you would, Mr. Haxhiu. "Q. Did that person introduce himself as an investigator of the OTP? "A. Yes." Now, tell me: Why did you tell this Court you were not an investigator when in fact you were, and you introduced yourself to Mr. Haxhiu as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question assumes facts which are not in evidence. I think he first needs to ask the witness whether he accepts and the extent to which he accepts the witness's -- the other witness's answer in a previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're -- yeah, thank you, Mr. Stamp. We're into this technical area of how you put a prior, inconsistent statement, Mr. O'Sullivan. I think, strictly speaking, the point made by Mr. Stamp are right. There are two questions in there and you have to take them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu has testified under oath that you introduced yourself to him as an investigator. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen Mr. Haxhiu's testimony, but I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Well, why did you introduce yourself as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not. We're talking here, Mr. Stamp, about something that's in a transcript. Are you questioning the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm not questioning the transcript. This is -- to ask the question: Why did you introduce yourself as an investigator assumes that the witness accepts what that previous witness said. I think we have to get over that hurdle first. Do you accept that you introduced yourself as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I suppose technically, Mr. O'Sullivan, that's not the question you asked him. So perhaps you should ask him that question just for the avoidance of doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, one thing must be clear that what would be this big difference between an investigator and a researcher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you need to answer that question for the moment. Let's proceed to deal with the evidence that we're exploring. And I think the question you have to ask first of all, Mr. O'Sullivan, is whether the witness accepts that that's how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, can you answer the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I do not recall how I introduced myself to Mr. Haxhiu. There may also be some misunderstanding because Mr. Haxhiu and I speak in both English and Albanian, so there could be a language complication. And there could also be a misunderstanding on Mr. Haxhiu's part or -- in not knowing the distinction between the two. But I do not recall precisely how I presented myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not pressing the other question then on the assumption that he did introduce himself as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I believe he's already accepted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. I have a few questions for you, to follow up the questions put by my colleague. Today and in some of your statements you've described your work for the OTP of this Tribunal. In those statements you mentioned the analysis you prepared for the OTP. What is contained in those analyses? What issues did you deal with and are those analyses concluded with conclusions?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- I had two primary tasks during my time with the Prosecutor's office. The first was to collect documents in Kosovo after the war left behind by either the MUP or VJ, the police or army. The second task was to identify Kosovar Albanian political negotiators, individuals who had contact during or prior to the war with Serbian government officials or Yugoslav government officials in the various phases of negotiations that took place in 1998 and 1999, to determine from these individuals information they had about the negotiation process. Those were my two primary jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While you were employed by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, did you also work with your home organisation, the Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I kept the two distinctly separate. And I will elaborate very briefly based on the previous question. While I was working here at the Tribunal, the report Under Orders was in the phase of editing. And as I mentioned yesterday, the editing process is lengthy and rigorous, especially with a report of that magnitude. So it took many months for the various reviewers to complete their reading. And it was during that time that I was here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we try to keep your answers as brief as possible so as to economise. Perhaps you can clearly focus on what my question was. In some of your public appearances, and can I remind you if need be which those are, you also questioned the mode or the way used by the investigators of this Tribunal to approach the events in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you refer me to the statement or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P385. Could that be shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is your report, or your article, I don't know what exactly I would call it. You authored that for the War & Peace Reporting?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the one shown here is in B/C/S. I think the copy should be in English for the Court and B/C/S for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Could we have the English version on e-court, please. The last two pages of this document, please. I would kindly ask that the witness be shown those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect that if you've got numbers for these last two pages, you should give these to assist. I don't mean an ERN number, I mean numbers in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 9 and 10, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that page 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 10. This is page 10, Your Honour. Can we have the previous page, number 9, please? Actually, number 8, please. Page number 8. I do apologise, Your Honour. These are just teething problems with this new system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this your article, Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect we'll be at the dentist until the trial's over, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it does seem to me that that is the case, but we are doing our very best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Abrahams, what is this, what is this article about? Who was it written for?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics of this article, but based on the document it is something that I wrote for the Institute for War & Peace Reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As we don't have it on the screen, I don't want us to waste any more time and to scroll down -- or perhaps if you would be so kind as to scroll this page down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again. Can we have the next page, namely page number 9, please. The fourth paragraph on page number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here you refer to new enthusiasm of western governments and commitment to international justice, the enthusiasm of western governments which happened to emerge all of a sudden from the beginning of the NATO bombing campaign and did not exist before that. Wherefrom in your judgement did that enthusiasm spring? Why did you write this -- and in fact this is some sort of a criticism of the attitude of those governments before that period?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very much a criticism of those governments. Human Rights Watch had been advocating on governments to provide the necessary resources to this Tribunal to allow it to perform its mandated task. And we were -- we welcomed the attention the Tribunal received in 1999 and wished that it had come, well, prior to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that context you are calling in question the fact that the majority of the investigators of the International Tribunal who were active in Kosovo after the NATO forces entered Kosovo were precisely the investigators from NATO member states. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My -- this article does not refer to that in particular. It refers to western governments, financial support for -- to fund the Office of the Prosecutor and the Tribunal in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll this page down a bit further, please, and take a look at the third paragraph from the bottom, where you say: The use of investigators from countries who were parties to the conflicts such as the US and the UK risks undermining the Tribunal's credibility as an objective judicial organ and even creating a sense of victor's justice.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand corrected, I did not recall this article well enough to remember that paragraph, but I stand by what I've written here. In my view, the Tribunal's credibility in the Balkan region in Yugoslavia is of utmost importance. It must make all efforts to appear balanced and independent. And having investigators from non-NATO countries would have, in my view, improved that image.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then, as you were actively involved in the different stages of the work, I can really say on this case, can you tell me who were the people who were in charge of the investigation on behalf of the Tribunal in the Kosovo case? What were they by nationality? What countries did they come from? I'm sure that you know that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosovo team was large and changed over time, but I recall that it was run by a Brit, but it had participation of -- of police investigators from numerous countries such as Italy, Australia, Pakistan, Great Britain, and I would have to think longer about other countries that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of this Brit? What were the names of his assistant, of his deputy? What countries did they come from, if you can help us with that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as a matter of clarification, I assume this is not confidential information of the Tribunal. I'm not aware of what I'm allowed to reveal if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think if it was you would have a Prosecutor on his feet objecting to the evidence. So I think you can assume that there's nothing confidential in the question that you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The director of the Kosovo research was Dennis Milner, and his deputy, who I believe assumed chief responsibility in the second -- in my second period with the Tribunal was Kevin Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And these two gentlemen are both British, right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then in the light of this observation of yours, which I think is quite appropriate, don't you think that this is indeed victor's justice, where you have justice being investigated by people who are actively involved in the matter which they seek to investigate on behalf of their countries? This is precisely what you state in your article. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that at all. My article is referring to the image and repetition of the Tribunal as an independent body, which would have been promoted by a more diverse staff. However, in my view both Mr. Milner and Mr. Curtis, as well as the other investigators, performed their role in a very professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please just give me a brief answer then. Why do you think then that the bringing of such people to such positions actually is risking undermining the credibility of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the eyes of Yugoslav citizens, they could view the Tribunal as a partisan institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I have a problem with the computer. The image seems to have been lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Help should be at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is all right now. Thank you. Can the witness please be shown document P2228. This is a set -- a batch of his statements that he gave in several instances, because we are going to be discussing those so that they should be at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want him to have a hard copy of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if view of the nature of my questions, I don't think that will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement, the one from 2002, you have an entire series of facts that you adduce from the history of Kosovo and Metohija. What are these sources on the basis of which in this second statement of yours, i.e., in the documents that you were preparing, that you used to produce those documents?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you're referring to the statements on Kosovo's history specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were numerous sources, public records such as speeches or the memorandum from the Academy of Science, for example, plus articles and analysis written by Yugoslav citizens and foreigners, as well as my interviews and knowledge from multiple visits to the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if you consulted such numerous sources, how is it then possible that on page 12 of this document that I indicated you state that the constitution from 1974 gave Kosovo the status of an autonomous province within the SFRY? What was the source that you consulted? Where did you find that particular bit of information?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we just find precisely where in the document that is said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, page 12 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The ERN page number -- I beg your pardon, the e-court page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] E-court number 12 in this document that I referred to earlier, P2228. Unfortunately that's not it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's page 13 he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I accept that and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the first sentence in the second paragraph that we can see on the e-court screen.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry that I do not recall the precise source from which this information was derived, but the changes of the 1974 constitution, namely granting autonomous status to both Kosovo and Vojvodina, is a publicly known and widely documented fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question had to do with a notoriously false claim that is contained in paragraph 2 in this. It is not true that Kosovo became an autonomous province in 1974, and it was not within Yugoslavia that it became a province; it was in the Republic of Serbia. And that is where the problem is. If you can comment on that; if not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you are correct. It was a province within Serbia. I know you are correct. I think the phrasing of this paragraph is open to that interpretation. It was autonomous within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware of the fact that Kosovo's autonomy within -- that Kosovo had been autonomous within Serbia as of 1946? At that particular point in time it had been autonomous for a full 30 years. It was nothing new that was granted to Kosovo in relation to its status that it had throughout the post-Second World War period?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not knowledgeable about the pre-1974 constitutional arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right then. When you talk about the alleged abolishment of its autonomy by the 1989 constitutional amendments, you are not aware of the true and substantive nature of the constitutional amendments that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of the particularities in the constitutional amendments, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the details of the amendments; I'm talking about -- I'm asking you about the constitutional concept of the abolishment of the autonomy. Of course I don't expect you to know the particulars of the constitutional changes, when and where and how they took place. I'm just asking you about the key fact, the abolishment, the emergence of something -- the granting of something that you say was done in 1974 and was abolished in 1989. I'm just asking you about the general concept.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but what would you like me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that all your allegations in this context are incomplete, incorrect, and superficial?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not accept that. I believe this -- my statement accurately reflects the broad strokes of constitutional developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I submit to you that that is not true, but in view of the nature of your testimony we are not going to dwell on this. In your statements you also refer to the fact that in the period from the 1970s to the 1990s of the past century, a large number of Serbs moved out from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. You say that they were exposed to maltreatment, that not always steps were taken to protect them, and so on and so forth. So my question is: Did your organisation ever investigate that particular phenomenon which so dramatically marked an entire epoch in Serbia and the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My organisation came into existence in 1977 with a very limited activity due to small size, primarily focussed at first on the Soviet Union. And our first work in Yugoslavia was, if I'm not mistaken, in 1990. However, the period of discrimination against Serbs that you mention is covered subsequently in the reports as background.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, for instance, in the 1980s when your organisation was very active in the countries of the former eastern bloc and in other countries with a socialist system, you were not interested in the position and the human rights status of the Kosovo Serbs which obviously were dramatically jeopardised in the period under review?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are dozens of countries and issues that we would like to investigate around the world at any time, and I could list them currently, but we do not have the resources or ability to conduct investigations in them all. I will say that we did engage ourselves, to some extent, in Yugoslavia by protesting the arrests of political prisoners. Of particular note is -- I recall a protest letter on behalf of Vojislav Seselj, who was put in prison in the 1980s for political reasons, which we protested. So we were involved, to some extent, but not in in-depth investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To conclude, to wrap up this particular topic, the moving out of several hundreds of thousands of people was not a topic which you thought worthy of your activity in the 1980s, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question's been answered. I do not think that's on appropriate further question to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell this Honourable Court who Robert Gelbard is.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robert Gelbard is a top -- or was in the late 1990s, a top American diplomat. I don't recall his precise position. And I don't know what he's doing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was the assessment of the activity of the so-called liberation army of Kosovo given by Robert Gelbard in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Gelbard made two statements that I am aware of in late February 1998, and maybe also early March, in which he said the Kosovo Liberation Army was a terrorist group. This was about one week -- this was about one week prior to the first series of events in the Drenica valley --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please confine yourself to what my question is. I'm not asking you about the wider context; I'm just asking you about what his assessment was and what his attitude was in respect of the Kosovo Liberation Army. And do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very careful to avoid use of the term "terrorist." Instead, we referred to the Kosovo Liberation Army as an insurgent group, an insurgent army, a guerilla force, and we used those classifications when evaluating their respect for international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then -- but when we are talking about an organisation that -- which, as you state in numerous of your statements, kills, kidnaps, abducts, imprisoned people, plants bombs, why cannot it be called its right name? Why is not this practice given its right name? Why are euphemisms being used throughout a series of your statements and documents? Because all these are features of terroristic actions, an activity as referred to by Diplomat Gelbard.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my job and our job as an organisation is to document violations of IHL. We did that with regards to the KLA and used the appropriate terms that, in my view, do not impose interpretations and have connotations the way the term "terrorist" does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How is it -- how do you interpret then this difference between your own attitudes and those which were the official assessment of the US government at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are assumptions which are not warranted by the evidence. I don't think that's been accepted that these were official assessments. And secondly, the question asks him to read into the intentions and meanings of other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't accept that objection. The ambassador in office at the time can be said to be expressing an official viewpoint, and therefore I will repel that objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, firstly, I would note that despite Ambassador Gelbard's comments, the Kosovo Liberation Army was never added to the state department's list of terrorist organisations, so it never had the official designation. But even if it did, there were numerous times throughout the conflict when Human Rights Watch's views and the United States government's views were different. In fact, we criticised the United States government on numerous occasions. So the inconsistency that you are mentioning is consistent with our independent work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So is there a difference in assessments, in assessing someone who kills and kidnaps and plants bombs, and is it in that particular respect that you disagree with the US government? Can I understand your answer like that? I'm not talking about numerous other issues where differences are quite possible. I'm asking you about specifically this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The US government's role is to make political decisions, and my organisation's role is to document and publicise violations of IHL. So it was international law that guided our work in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I don't think that was the answer to my question. Perhaps you could try answering it. If the US government deems certain actions to be of terrorist nature and if your views differ, do you accept then that your position is different from the position of the US government, which calls someone terrorist when they plant bombs, kill, and abduct, whereas you did not accept that? Perhaps you have another name for such activities. If this is so, what is that name?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We refrained from using the term or the word "terrorist" or "terrorism." I think the US government on numerous occasions vocally criticised the IHL violations by the Kosovo Liberation Army -- by all forces in the conflict. I do not believe they used the word "terrorist" after Ambassador Gelbard did. But again, we refrain from using a term that we consider loaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I -- I accept that this is a perfectly valid line of inquiry and a perfectly proper submission will be made in due course, no doubt, about the use of language reflecting attitude. But I note that to the same question earlier the witness said that the answer was that they were referred to as insurgent groups, which is an interesting expression in view of the use of that expression currently, and guerilla forces. Now, is there really much more mileage in this line of examination at this stage with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully accept your comment and I will move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ambassador Gelbard in March expressed his attitude as to the -- as concerns the activities of the KLA. Later on you write the US government changed its assessment of the KLA, although the KLA modus operandi did not change. It even became more drastic. First of all, do you know of that change of designation for that group in the official statements of the US government?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My only knowledge to that effect is the comments made by Ambassador Gelbard and the subsequent fact that the KLA was not added to the statement department's list of terrorist organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The fact that only several months after the statement by the Ambassador Gelbard another highly positioned American diplomat, Mr. Holbrooke, visited a headquarters of the KLA, legitimising their modus operandi and their organisation. What do you think that impact -- what impact that had on the situation in the field? How would you term such a change? What impact did it have on the ground, particularly concerning the events that took place?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give you my interpretation or my analysis of how that event impacted Kosovo. Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion the US government, and Ambassador Holbrooke in particular, were searching for ways to resolve the conflict through political negotiations, and there was reluctance at first to contact the Kosovo Liberation Army - in my view, my interpretation of the government's actions - out of fear of legitimising them. However, at some point the US government apparently realised that the KLA was a relevant factor, that the KLA was not going to go away, and that no political solution could be achieved by relying only on Ibrahim Rugova and his LDK party, therefore leading Holbrooke to establish contact at that time in the village of Junik, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My last question concerning the topic will be the following. How do you assess the fact that someone who did not change their modus operandi, not moving away from the essentially terrorist way of action, all of a sudden turned into a legitimate collocutor, partner? What would be your view of legitimising such an organisation which used clearly terrorist methods in its work?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again we refrain from using the word "terrorist," but in my view there are two distinct processes. There are political negotiations and there is due process. So the crimes committed by the Kosovo Liberation Army, which we have also documented, the abductions, the expulsions, the murders, should be punished either in a Kosovo court or an international tribunal, without any question. What happens politically and who engages in negotiations is another matter. And in our view, those two are separate and distinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have a question, or perhaps it might be deemed a comment, but perhaps nevertheless you could comment. It seems that if you are numerous enough and persistent enough you may become a legitimate collocutor. Would you assess US policy towards organisations in that way?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it was poorly interpreted. If one uses violence for a sufficiently long time and intensively enough, that organisation or person would be a legitimate partner in a political process. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question generally. In the Kosovo case, it became clear to me, personally, based on work in the field, that the KLA was a relatively large organisation and an armed force, a structured and functioning armed force, and that no solution to the crisis could be found without their involvement in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the means used to attain that goal?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. You mean the goal of engaging the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, sir. We are talking about the process of legitimising the activities of the KLA. Such a status is accorded, provided one uses violence persistently and systematically enough.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak from the perspective of my organisation on this, which is our job is not to legitimise or delegitimise anyone. Our job is to research the facts on the ground. So we engage with all relevant actors, governmental and non-governmental.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on. We are still with the P2228 document. Page 18 in e-court, that's page 18 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it before me yet. I hope I'm correct about the numbers. Page 18, please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, as it was on the screen before you scrolled down. This is fine. Now the last paragraph. [In English] "During the second quarter of 1998 ..." [Interpretation] There you state that: "During the second quarter of 1998, the KLA took control of an estimated 40 per cent of Kosovo's territory." Then: "Serb civilians in areas under KLA control were harassed or terrorised into leaving their homes, by assaults, kidnapping, and sporadic killing." This is what you stated then, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate of the total percentage -- of the percentage of the total population living in that particular part of Kosovo where we see the 40 per cent mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. However, the areas of control -- the areas under KLA control were largely rural areas with the exception of the town of Malisevo. So I would -- I would expect the percentage of Kosovo's population to be relatively small. Or at least less than 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't have a precise estimate, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: By occupying 40 per cent of Kosovo's territory during the relevant time, being -- [In English] "Second quarter of 1998 ..." [Interpretation] The second quarter of 1998, as stated, would the 40 per cent encompass those parts of Kosovo through which the main arteries, the main roads go connecting the east and the west of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some areas, yes. However, I used the term "loose control" because to the best of my knowledge the government still maintained control of the main arteries. The KLA may have had them for brief periods or during the evenings or night-times, but the roads were throughout this period open and under the control of government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the main roads from Pristina to Pec or from Pristina to Prizren were open? Was any traffic possible? Could civilians or food be transported along those roads?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe for most of that time the roads were open, although it is possible they were closed for specific periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many attacks were conducted along those roads in the relevant period, the attacks by the KLA on military, police, and civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. We requested that information from the authorities but received no reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us from where or from whom you sought such information and who denied you an answer?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following my research mission in Kosovo in spring, May/June, of 1998, in July I sent letters to various government authorities asking for information about attacks on Serbian civilians. I believe those letters also include a question about police and Yugoslav casualties during that time. But I would have to check the letters to be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You are talking here about road communication, about whether roads were open. Did you address anyone with that question? Because those roads, the ability to communicate along those roads meant the free movement of people, transportation of goods, and essentially survival.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those letters I referred to did not ask specific questions about roads, and I do not recall if I otherwise inquired particularly about traffic communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. Did you know that two large towns in Kosovo were completely besieged at that time, the two being Decani and Djakovica, without any means or ability to communicate with the outside world? Of course, they were encircled by the KLA units.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that KLA was active in and around Decan. They were also active around Djakovica, but I am not aware of -- of Djakovica being besieged, as you say. There may have been individual incidents in Djakovica, but to my knowledge the town was largely opening and functioning throughout the period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many attacks were there in late spring and early fall against the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslav police and military?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the precise number I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any framework data at least, approximately? And if not, why -- why didn't you bother to gather those? Why didn't you turn to the authorities? Why didn't you use your personnel to gather data which in turn was important for the research you were doing?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We requested that data from the various authorities in Belgrade but received no reply. So we were forced to rely on secondary sources, such as media reports for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And concerning those secondary sources, I presume you consulted the press in Pristina and Belgrade. If indeed you researched and you used those sources, what were your conclusions? How many attacks? How many victims? Where?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We referred to the sources you mention as well as international press. And we have written in our report that at least 100 ethnic Serbs -- ethnic Serb civilians went missing, went missing during the first half of 1998 -- or to be more precise, throughout 1998. These were civilians who lived in areas that the KLA had under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I thank you for that piece of information, but I wanted to ask you something else. The research you did, what was the data you gathered? How many attacks against the police? How many attacks on the police -- on the military? How many attacks on civilians and civilian trucks or vehicles and where? It was in the media daily, since you say you did not have any other source apart from the media. What results did your research come up with?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attacks on the media -- excuse me. Attacks on the military are of interest to us to better understand the conflict, but they are not of concern in -- in our evaluations because military and police are legitimate military targets. I would qualify that a little bit by saying that the method and means of attack is very important to determine if it was proportionate and discriminate. But we, in the Kosovo case, focussed our attention on the impact of the war on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, we do speak different languages, but it appears to me what I'm asking you is interpreted correctly. Perhaps you were not interested in the police and the army, but what was the number of attacks on civilians and civilian vehicles in the relevant time? There were people, women, children who were moving from Djakovica to Pristina. How many attacks were there against those? Do you know that? Were you interested in that? And does that include incidents that may be of interest to your organisation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you summary statistics. I do not know how many attacks took place at the time. I can give you some specific incidents that we investigated. For example, the abduction by the KLA of approximately 80, I believe 85, Serbian civilians in the town of Orahovac. Subsequently, they released approximately 40 of them. 35 of them are still missing today and are presumed dead. I can mention the abduction of ten Serbian employees of the Belacevac mine who are still missing today and who are presumed dead. I can mention the abduction of various individuals and families throughout Kosovo. So I can give you that information, but I don't have a total figure to present you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree that the attacks I mentioned came in dozens or in hundreds perhaps? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more precise. Attacks on civilians or on armed forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Attacks on civilian vehicles, civilian means of transport, attacks on the military which was not in action, attacking police patrols, or attacking other state bodies and people employed by the state, such as forest rangers, mailmen. Would you agree with me if I said that such attacks came in hundreds?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to give you a number, but I will agree that the KLA was active during that time in both attacking military targets as well as engaging in IHL violations like expelling, abducting, or killing some Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you would agree that their activities were very widespread. Such attacks appeared on almost one-half of the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the KLA was -- was an active insurgent force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave we could have a break now because I am about to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We'll resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I have a question which stems from the previous part which we were discussing before the recess. If you can give me an answer, please, to my question regarding attacks on the military, on the army, and on the police in the period under consideration, you responded that it was not a matter of your interest, that you did not deal with that, and that attacks on the army and police were legitimate targets and therefore not a subject of your own investigations. Can you explain to me, please, how is it possible that an attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't think that's an accurate reflection of the evidence. The witness explained that they were interested in any disproportionate conduct against the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How is it at all possible to legitimately attack the army and the police in conditions of an absence of a state of war when there does not exist a state of war, when there were no overt armed conflicts? How is it possible to do that in a legitimate way under such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our analysis as an organisation, we determined that a state of armed conflict existed in Kosovo from late February/beginning of March 1998. This was based on our analysis of the facts on the ground and the existence of the KLA as an adequately organised armed force. So given that fact, we conducted our analysis with a focus on the war's impact on civilians. Does that answer your question adequately?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I just want to understand your attitude, your position. So it is your position that in an organised state one may legitimately attack the army and the police, and that can even be legally characterised as an armed conflict. Is that your position on this issue?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of international humanitarian law is that such attacks are not forbidden. It is the manner of attack which is evaluated under the law. However, however, however, my understanding is also that in what's known as an internal armed conflict, attacks by an insurgent group can be prosecuted under domestic law. So the Serbian and Yugoslav authorities were legally able to arrest and prosecute individuals who they believed had committed criminal acts, such as the illegal possession of arms, kidnappings, or murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Or an attack on members of the army or of the police as well?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any information - and we are still in 1998 - about the strength of the KLA, how many members did it have? How were they organised?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What month in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about June, July, August 1998.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the KLA was still a disparately organised armed group. My understanding from that time and from subsequent research is that it was highly decentralised so that there was a central command, but authority rested, to a great extent, with the regional commanders in the field. We did notice some unified policies. For example, by September of 1998 it was necessary to obtain what I believe they call the media pass, but it was essentially a document that allowed individuals to travel into the territory controlled by the KLA. And individuals were checking at -- there were check-points that controlled these documents. So this suggested to us an extent of coordination and control at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many members did the KLA have at that time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know how many members the KLA had, how then do you derive your conclusions about the adequacy of the response of the state defence forces throughout your report; namely, you have allegations about the disproportionate response of these forces. What is proportionate in your book if you do not have a number to compare it to in terms of the strength of the units of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the answer that was given earlier was about disproportionate action by the KLA, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So don't read it into the earlier answer that this has been -- that it was necessary for there to be knowledge about their numbers. I think this is a separate question, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, was the response, the reaction, of the defence -- state defence forces of Serbia and of Yugoslavia proportionate to the threat which was posed to it by KLA forces in at least 40 per cent of Kosovo territory?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, based on the investigations on the ground, the response of the government forces was highly disproportionate and had a indiscriminate method that impacted civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, this is not what I'm asking you. Mr. Abrahams, I'm not asking you that. What I am asking you is that can you conclude that the reaction, the response, of the forces of the army and the police was adequate to the existing threat? I'm not asking you about anything which encroaches upon the domain of international humanitarian law. I'm talking about legitimate military and police action. Was it proportionate to the existing threat?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interest is not if a government responds to a security threat that it perceives; my interest is how that government responds to the security threat. That was the focus of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in your work and in your statements, in your documents, there is nothing about whether the reaction to the security threat was adequate or not. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adequate in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Adequate I explained in the previous question. Adequacy in the sense of the threat posed to the security of the state which is reflected in the fact that someone has occupied, for instance, 40 per cent of the territory of one of its provinces.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an active armed insurgency in Kosovo. From the perspective of the Serb and Yugoslav authorities, that was a threat to their security. We acknowledge that, I acknowledge that, and my interest was in how the state responded to that perceived threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. In this same statement from 2002 of yours from July, we are talking about the period immediately after these events in June, July, and August, and there on page 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we see page 20 in e-court, please. Can you scroll down a bit, please. Just bear with me for a minute, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As unfortunately I cannot find it here, I'm going to read it out, a part of your statement. I hope you will be able to recognise it and immediately respond to my question which will follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course by leave to the Court, if they will allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "In August the Serbian government opened 11 humanitarian centres in Kosovo for the rendition of aid. A very small number of Albanians came to receive aid. I met many Albanians who were afraid to approach representatives of the Serbian government in view of the vehements of the violence they had been exposed to." Do you remember this paragraph from your statement?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what this humanitarian relief which the Yugoslav authorities wanted to provide the population with contained?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concretely, no, but I understood it to be food and possibly health supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it stem from what I've read out to you that this aid was intended for all needy inhabitants, irrespective of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the stated aim of this project, but in my opinion it was not a sincere effort on the part of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is it that brings you -- leads you to the conclusion that it was not a sincere effort on the part of the government, since in your statement you go on to say, and I can read it also out for you that: "A multitude of the inhabitants of Albanian ethnicity did not want to take that aid precisely for fear of the reaction of KLA members."

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's a misrepresentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we just find what part of the statement that apparent quote is taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can find it. Just a minute, please. Just one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that it is easier to read this in B/C/S than try to find it in English, which I will certainly bear in mind during my next stint of questioning. And I shall certainly have the English version. So, with your permission, I shall read the 2002 statement. The first paragraph is the one I just read, and immediately following is this paragraph. "During that period the KLA, as well as in the beginning of 1999, committed grave violations of humanitarian law, including -- including the taking of hostages and summary executions. Their victims were Albanians and Serbs who -- Serbs and Albanians who were thought to have been collaborating."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down when he's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down when you read, Mr. Petrovic. But that paragraph doesn't bear the statement which was in your question, that the Albanians did not resort to the aid centres because of fear of reaction of KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is of course true, but that is the following paragraph. Now I'm talking about the first paragraph, the first paragraph which talks about humanitarian relief centres, but already in the next paragraph shows what fate awaits an Albanian if he cooperates with the Serbian state in any way whatsoever. So I have linked the two paragraphs, in view of the fact that they are simply parts of the one and same context. So I hope that the witness will be able to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Abrahams, when you say: "I met many Albanians who were afraid to approach the Serbian authorities given the level of violence they had experienced," what was the violence to which you were referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were referring to the violence inflicted upon them by Serbian and Yugoslav forces, which -- in other words, they were being offered help in their eyes from the people who evicted them from their homes in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, can you now reply to the question which I put to you, and I can repeat it. What was the influence of the fact that the KLA was maltreating and killing Albanians who were cooperating with the Serbian state on the possibility for those people who of course needed help, Albanians in need of help, to indeed accept such help from the Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The individuals I interviewed expressed concern and fear from the state authorities. However, I do accept your point that there was intimidation in general on the ethnic Albanian population from the KLA. And it is possible that some villagers or some individuals were instructed not to participate in this humanitarian aid effort. Nobody testified to me to that effect, but I accept that it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what kind of an organisation is World Vision?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, World Vision is a US-based humanitarian organisation with ties to the church, although which church in particular I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did this organisation provide any assistance in February 1999 in Kosovo in terms of the reconstruction of houses and things like that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: World Vision was definitely active in Kosovo, also in house -- home reconstruction, but I do not know what date they began their operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this activity of theirs and this assistance in home reconstruction, was it possible without the consent and the cooperation of the authorities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a question for World Vision. My assumption is such cooperation is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, and please bear with me for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown document P386, Kosovo: Rape as a Weapon of 'Ethnic Cleansing.' Just one minute, Your Honour, I'm looking for the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please -- this is a book which contains your analysis of instances of rape in Kosovo alleged to have taken place in the period we are considering, right? Do you remember the statement by the foreign secretary of Britain at the time, Mr. Robin Cook, about the existence of some camps, as he referred to them, for raped women in March and April 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those statements, in general. I don't recall the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I shall ask you now to look at page -- page 10 in e-court. In the document itself it is page 8, but in e-court it is page 10. So here -- actually -- actually, the next page, the ERN number of which is 828, please, not this one, which is 827. The following page, please. Yes. Well, here you see the first paragraph. Can you tell us, please, when was it that Robin Cook gave this statement, made this claim?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report, it was April 13th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about your report, that was your report prepared on behalf of the organisation that you belonged to, right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
