utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So on the 13th of April, 1999, Robin Cook, the British foreign secretary, claimed that Serbian forces had opened a rape hotel or a rape camp near Djakovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what were the conclusions of your organisation in connection with this specific claim of Mr. Cook's?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not collect information or evidence to confirm this allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate these allegations?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the conclusion was that what Robin Cook had said was untrue?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not able to find the evidence to support his claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the impact of the rumours about rapes on these -- on the inhabitants of a certain portion of territory? How is it that you describe that in your reports?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our view was and is that there were very serious incidents of sexual violence and rape committed against ethnic Albanian civilians at that time, based on our information --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask the witness to respond to my question. I wanted to know what the impact of rumours was. Perhaps the witness could contain his answer to what I asked him, and the rest was contained in examination-in-chief and it can be found in the report, which may or may not be later admitted. I don't want to waste our time; therefore, I would like to stay focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have to object to the question as it was first put and as it is now put. A question, what is the impact of rumours is impermissibly vague and it leaves the witness at large. The question should be a little more focussed, it is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that question is something which is -- that is encompassed in the reports we are discussing and stems directly from my previous question. Mr. Robin Cook stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your question confined to what Cook said, being unfounded on the face of it? Is that what you're describing as a rumour?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's the rumour, then that's what the question relates to, and the -- the point that's being made is no more than that. So the question is: What was the effect of this allegation which turned out to be, following Mr. Abrahams's investigation, apparently unfounded on the community. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was in the process of answering that very question. Because of the serious crimes of sexual violence we documented, we were then very concerned, troubled, by allegations from political actors that appeared unfounded or not based on fact because it then eroded the credibility of the actual crimes that were committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that doesn't answer the question that's being put to you, which is: What impact did it have in the community in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in part, it may have had that impact, to dilute the facts that were proved in the course of investigations. In addition, there may have been a -- in my opinion, there was a political impact, and I can only -- I can only suppose Robin Cook's intention, which at that time was to muster support, political support, for the NATO endeavour. And I can only assume that his comments in this regard were intended in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. I'm Norman Sepenuk, and I'm one of the attorneys for General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher would put on the screen the Prosecution Exhibit 544, page 2. I take it it's on your screen, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Abrahams, you have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you'll recognise that, sir, as a letter of July 20, 1998, by Holly Cartner, the executive director for Human Rights Watch for Europe and Central Asia. And as I understand it from your testimony, you actually drafted this letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it was signed by Ms. Cartner.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you scroll down to the signature, I can respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Can we do that, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, but based on the -- my personal analysis of my own handwriting that I signed this letter in the name of Ms. Cartner as she deputised me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that's actually your signature?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is I believe my signature, but we would have to perform an analysis of the handwriting to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We don't need an expert, I can assure you. And this letter, was it your idea to send this letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter is standard operating procedure following missions to request information from the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I believe you said yesterday you would characterise it as a letter of inquiry?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's a proper -- proper description, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That was your testimony yesterday. Fair enough? Letter of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So there's nothing in this letter, I take it, which you would characterise in -- at all as any kind of a charge or -- an implicit charge of violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean directing to the authorities specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Anything in this letter. Let's just take an example. The first question is: "How many VJ soldiers have died in Kosovo since January 1998? How many have been wounded?" Okay. These are requesting -- these are factual matters. You want answers --

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- correct? Okay. And if you would just assist us just for a moment in putting this matter in context, the letter was dated July 20, 1998, and if we can just back up a little bit and go to the end of the second quarter of 1998, which is right in that ballpark, it was in that period that the KLA took loose control, at least, of an estimated 40 per cent of Kosovo's territory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And further during that period Serb civilians in areas under KLA control were harassed or terrorised into leaving their homes by assaults, kidnappings, and sporadic killings. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it's further correct, is it not, that the day before this letter was sent on July 19th, 1998, the KLA's first major offensive began when it attempted to capture the town of Orahovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. So the letter is dated July 20, 1998. An awful lot was going on, wasn't it, at that period?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. The day before the attack on Orahovac, right, and then again 40 per cent of the territory being controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So Serb authorities had a lot to do during that period?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assumedly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And yet you gave them a ten-day limit to reply to their letter. You sent it during the vacation period, July 20, and then gave them a ten-day limit to reply. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to see the precise date on the end of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's right there, actually.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does that say "July"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just leave it right there. Right.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you scroll to the right? It's cut off, but I assume it is July, yes. Yes, that's correct, then we gave them a ten-day time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Ten-day time-frame to respond; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you e-mail the letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is this letter was faxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It was faxed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And again, as I understand it, there was no response?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And did you then ask -- what's the closest human rights office to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geographically probably Brussels at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you're confident that the fax arrived?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am confident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You have a record of that? Are you testifying to that, that you have a record that exists that shows that the fax arrived?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, I should explain the procedure of distributing these letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are sent through a fax server on a computer, which dials the number and does not stop dialing until the fax is successfully delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And when you didn't get an answer within a few days, was there any thought given to perhaps hand-delivering the letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall if there was thought given to it, but my recollection is that it was never delivered physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't make any phone calls about it to anybody in the army, I take it?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall at that time. However, many of these issues were also raised in person when I had a meeting with Mr. Bosko Drobnjak in Pristina during my research mission. And I requested specific information from him, which he said he was not authorised to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you'd already discussed a number of the matters contained in this letter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go through the specifics of the letter to determine precisely what I had discussed with Mr. Drobnjak or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, you met with Mr. Drobnjak on June 11th, 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check my records, but that sounds correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I represent that to you. I'm reading from your statement.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he was with the Serb -- Serbian Ministry of Information in Pristina; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he didn't refuse to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He accepted to speak with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you had a rather wide-ranging conversation?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it was a 30- to 45-minute conversation on current affairs in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he talked to you about a number of topics; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about -- would you like to know specifically if I can recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sure. Whatever your recollection is, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that Mr. Drobnjak referred to the KLA as a terrorist organisation, as terrorists. I recall that he said the Serbian and Yugoslav forces were responding appropriately. And I asked in particular two questions. One was reports about the state authorities blocking the delivery of humanitarian aid to ethnic Albanian populations, and he replied that the government had done so because some of these organisations were delivering supplies to the -- to the KLA, although he was not able to provide any specifics. And secondly, if my memory serves me correctly, I submitted to him a list of ethnic Albanians that were missing and asked for his -- any information he had about those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So Mr. Drobnjak essentially defended the government position. Is that an fair statement?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an accurate representation of his position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he claimed that the Serb authorities were fighting terrorists and their actions were justified?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then further in this letter you asked the army -- I'll call it the army, again you never had any discussions with any specific person, did you, at the time this letter was sent?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. All right. You just sent it to the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's sent to the information service of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, and that's -- I'm sorry, where is that listed?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's on the cover sheet of the fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Could we just see that for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That would be page 1?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Information service; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Drobnjak was the -- with the Serbian Ministry of Information; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, I mean, he's authorised to speak to you about these matters. And you had spoken to him in June?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the questions was: "Can you provide us with any military reports about the actions of the army in Kosovo since January 1998?" Did you really expect, I ask seriously not frivolously, did you really expect to get military reports from the government? Don't you think there's some element of confidentiality there that the government might not be willing to share with Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my job to ask questions and the government's job to determine what it answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But confidentiality within any organisation, particularly where lives are at stake, particularly given this -- this warfare between the KLA and Yugoslav forces, would be very important; correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been surprised had the military replied to us with internal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. So you asked the question, but you really, as a practical matter, didn't expect to get a response, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that specific question, I would have been surprised to obtain military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And -- and that same confidentiality, I take it, is something that is very important to your organisation, Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confidentiality in what regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, for example, of reports, of interviews.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference between reports and interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. Let me say interviews. As I understand it, the book Under Orders was essentially based on interviews of some 600 Kosovar Albanians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the period in that report that covers March to June 1999, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you stated that you chose individuals who you thought had stories to tell?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And then you amended that just a few seconds later and said you were "seeking out individuals who had knowledge of crimes." Correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You weren't seeking out anybody with exculpatory information; you were seeking out people with inculpatory information?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sought people who had stories to tell, and where those stories led we reported. And there are examples in Under Orders of Serbian police and Yugoslav army who responded properly, legally, morally. We included that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an example in the evidence presented before where we refuted information presented by Robin Cook. So we were very carefully to present also exculpatory information. And if we learned -- and maybe I can clarify my previous testimony to be absolutely clear on this. If we learned that an individual had exculpatory information, we would have also sought that person out. We actively sought individuals with knowledge of events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If you learn by chance, more or less, that there were individuals who had exculpatory information, then you would seek them out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Or if those individuals were brought to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you weren't seeking out individuals who had exculpatory information. To the contrary, as I understand your testimony, you were seeking out individuals who had knowledge of crimes?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowledge of crimes should -- maybe I will clarify. Knowledge of reported crimes. So that when we conduct an investigation in a specific village, we will cast a wide net, so to speak, to interview individuals, to collect documents, to visit the alleged crime scene, to obtain as broad a spectrum of information as possible, inculpatory or exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as you stated in answer to a question from His Honour yesterday, you -- strike that. Strike that. No, don't strike it. You were seeking leads, were you not? Judge Bonomy said you were seeking leads to further investigation, at the very least?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of our investigations, we, like journalists, would -- would seek leads, would follow leads, would pursue all tidbits of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then you worked for the Prosecutor for a period of time; correct? You've testified to that. 2000/2001?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I think it's fair to say -- or is it fair to say that you shared these leads with the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I mean, any -- I take it any that were inculpatory you saw fit to share with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you turn over your 600 reports of interview to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The written testimony, the written statements or notes from our interviews are the property of Human Rights Watch, and we do not share them outside the organisation without specific request. We provided to the Tribunal names of individuals upon that individual's approval as someone who might be of interest to them with knowledge of a particular incident. And we presented to the Tribunal our summary findings; namely, the reports that have been presented here today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Has any member of the OTP at any time ever requested you - "you" being Human Rights Watch or any representative thereof - for copies of these 600 interview statements?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There's been no request by Mr. Stamp or Mr. Hannis or anyone in connection with the OTP about turning over these forms? Are you sure about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Request -- you mean a request for us to provide the Prosecutor office --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any request, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp, maybe -- can you clarify something that we discussed yesterday? I thought such a request had indeed been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. We have had -- and I don't know if we should do this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have inquired of the witness as to the whereabouts of the documents, and the witness has told us how we can get the documents and we are in the process of doing that. We have not asked the witness for the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There have been discussions with Mr. Stamp at least as to the procedure to obtain these documents?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And given all the work of the OTP in securing indictments and building evidence in the case, you're saying that at no time did they want from you what could be a very valuable work product, 600 interview statements, upon which your book, Under Orders, was based?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is available is the data set, which is the coded information from those interviews, but the specific written statements I was not requested to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have you now provided the so-called data set to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, but I have to confirm this information, is that this data set is publicly available. I believe it is on the internet, but I have to confirm that fact. So whether the OTP has accessed it or utilised it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I would certainly make a request at this time from the Prosecution to make that available as well as all the interview statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what the position of your organisation or your former organisation is, sir, on releasing this information?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what is that position?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of policy, the notes are the private property of the organisation, but individuals or organisations can make specific requests to our legal office for release, which will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: While you were serving as a consultant and/or investigator for the OTP, did it ever occur to you at any time to say to any of the Prosecutors, any of the investigators of the OTP: Gee, we have these 600 interview statements, you ought to take a look at it. Did that ever occur to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly it did not. I felt -- for two reasons. First I felt that our findings, as presented in Under Orders and other reports, were adequate to give a proper indication of the evidence we collected. And secondly, that the -- the investigators of the OTP needed to conduct their own interviews, gather their own information so that they could use our reports as a guide, if you will, to determine the pattern of abuses, what villages might be of interest and which may not, but that ultimately those investigations needed to be done by their own investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So there was a preference then in favour of the OTP using your reports rather than the raw material itself, which were the interviews. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it played out. Also because we, as a matter of principle, do not release the statement themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And at the time that you were writing these reports, let's say from -- let's just take the period August 1998 on when you were writing various reports and right through till the end, I take it it's fair to say that you -- we really can't call you a disinterested observer of the process, can we?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on your understanding of the term "disinterested."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, isn't it fair to say that you had already concluded as early as August 1998 that the first priority for United States policy should be the indictment of Mr. Milosevic. You concluded that as early as August 1998, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, yes. I mean, I would have to know to what you are precisely referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I think you do, don't you, sir? Your article on the August 5th, 1998 Herald Tribune in which you say precisely that and which you were asked about at the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that argument -- that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That article. And that's what you said: "The first priority" -- on August 5th, 1998, "the first priority of US policy should be the indictment of Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did write that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that's the mind-set you had throughout -- from that time on at least when you were assembling information, writing reports, dealing with the OTP, and doing all of the processes, going through all the processes, that you have testified about.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not describe it as a mind-set. I would describe it as my opinion based on investigations in the field up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Abrahams. My name is Aleksander Aleksic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade, appearing on behalf of General Pavkovic. I have a few questions for you. First of all, I'd like to follow up on Mr. Sepenuk's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show P544 to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In responding to these questions you stated that as far as the other side was concerned, you basically authored the letter and upon -- and you co-signed that, together with Ms. Holly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You were authorised to sign it by her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the other side of the document, the other page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to see page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to the front page or the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, this seems to be a fax form. Can you tell us whose handwriting this is. It says "the armed forces of Yugoslav, Kosovo command, information service," and under that the information service in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that there was also a number of the facsimile to be entered there -- or actually the number to which the facsimile is being sent?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a space for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since you addressed the letter, so to say, wouldn't it have been usual for you or one of the people who worked with you to fill in the number to which you were supposed to send this?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the number is added and sometimes it is not. In this case it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So how are we to know what number received this facsimile? Do you have any proof of that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer that question, I would have to check our contact lists in New York to tell you which number this fax was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe I didn't follow the transcript closely enough, but didn't you say today that your closest office was in Brussels and that this was sent from Brussels? Perhaps I'm wrong, and in that case I apologise.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was our closest office, which is Brussels, but this fax and the other faxes were sent from New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I accept your explanation. Since you wrote this yourself, it says "the armed forces of Yugoslavia, Kosovo command information service." Is that correct? Do you know whether there was such a thing as Kosovo command within the armed forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing what I know today, I would have labelled it differently. I would have labelled it either information service of the 3rd Army or of the Pristina Corps. But based on my understanding and knowledge at that time, I addressed it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you know today, where is the command of the 3rd Army and where is the command of the Pristina Corps and their respective information services? Perhaps where they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know. My assumption is that there are offices both in Belgrade and in Pristina. Perhaps the 3rd Army is based in Nis, but I'm not -- I'm not aware of that precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: My last question concerning this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the second page of the document again, and its title -- or rather, to whom the letter was sent. If we go to the top left corner it says: "The armed forces of Yugoslavia, Kneza Milosa 33 Street, Belgrade 11000, Yugoslav." Is there a difference between the first and the second page as to who the letter was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I do seem to have another question concerning this document and several others which are identical to this one, being the letter of the 20th of July, 1998. I don't think it is in dispute - and perhaps I needn't go into the other two documents and to show them here, but the other two letters were addressed to a certain person. Perhaps you remember that, minister of information, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In this letter, however, on its second page, the only thing we find is the armed forces of Yugoslavia, Kneza Milosa Street, number 33?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for a possibility then that this letter was never received at the appropriate address because of the way it was addressed? Perhaps I was -- I hope I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My belief and my assumption is that this letter arrived. But can I confirm that it got to the Kosovo command, no, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. I have only one more question pertaining to your report, Under Orders. It is a general question; hence, we needn't have that put on the screen. In replying to one of the questions posed by Mr. Sepenuk you stated that the main source of the report were the interviews you conducted at a certain time with the Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And I wish to repeat that this is a general question, but I've read the Serb version -- the Serbian version, and in the footnotes there is no mention of any source. There is a mention of a date and place of interview -- or rather, when the statement was taken. And on some pages there are only initials.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We provide a footnote for every interview, and in many, if not most, of the interviews we provide the name of the interviewee, the date and place of the interview. But there are cases in Under Orders where the interviewee requested some form of protection out of fear for retaliation, because at the time in the period March through June 1999, the war was ongoing, the resolution of the conflict was unclear, and the interviewees had, in my opinion, a reasonable fear for retaliation, should we provide their name in full. That fear dissipated to an extent after June when Kosovo Albanians returned to their homes and had more reason to feel secure. So fewer individuals were concerned about providing their full identity. When they did request such protection, we provided it to them because harming or putting in danger any witness or victim is a matter of serious concern to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That is regards that period, I accept what you stated, although we cannot verify that information, since in the footnotes to your report there are no other things, apart from the place and date. Therefore, we can't verify that information for the very same reason.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify that those interviews took place and were recorded accurately, based on what those individuals told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have just one more question, Mr. Abrahams. In the footnotes of your report, to a great extent, you stated that you relied mainly -- mainly on the OSCE report called As Seen, As Told. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Could you refer me to the precise footnote you mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In numerous footnotes. For example, page 102, footnote 10, "see OSCE Kosovo: As Seen, As Told." There was something before that as well. Page 160, footnote 3, "see OSCE Kosovo: As Seen, As Told, Part I," then page 163, footnote 9, "see OSCE Kosovo: As Seen, As Told, first chapter, parts 21 to 30."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, I am going through the B/C/S version, but that should tally as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Then pages 216 to 226 of the OSCE report As Seen, As Told as mentioned in the following footnote and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to review Under Orders precisely to answer your question specifically, but I can provide a general response, which is the primary and essential source of material in that report is our interviews. We do cite secondary material such as the OSCE document, but primarily when it has a corroborative value. So we would not rely on it as the sole source of information or if there are any cases where we mention that, an OSCE report, we would specify that we had not conducted our own investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have my reasons for posing this question. They're procedurally linked to some other evidence and other witnesses and statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Abrahams. First of all, I should like to ask you, to the best of your recollection, in 1998 how many times did you visit the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- or rather, Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you went to Kosovo four times, right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Kosovo four times, and in each of those times, maybe three of the four, I also visited Belgrade. I would fly into Belgrade, travel to Kosovo, return to Belgrade, and fly home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me please in what period were you in Kosovo and how much time did you spend there each time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first trip was in May/June of 1998. I returned in September. Again, I believe in November. And if I'm not mistaken, again in December. I may be confusing the December trip with a February 1999 trip. I apologise for not being precise on that, on those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, you actually allow that perhaps you had only made three trips in 1998 and not four?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. I may -- it may have been four trips in the period 1998 and early 1999 leading up to the NATO bombing. I'm not sure of that fourth trip -- the timing of that fourth trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The first time that you came, you spent the entire month of May and June, right, or perhaps it was different?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That trip was approximately three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, yesterday you said that you had come in mid-September 1998, that you went there in mid-September, 1998. How long did you stay that time?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that trip was approximately three weeks. I can obtain the exact dates for you, if that's of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, no, it is okay. Just roughly. So three weeks. And the last time in 1998, your last trip, did that also last three weeks or was it shorter?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- yes, also approximately three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, these three trips, during these three trips -- three-week trips, how many communes, how many municipalities in Kosovo did you visit?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible for me to answer, but dozens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know first and foremost how many municipalities there are in Kosovo and that municipalities encompass a large number of small places, of villages? Do you make this distinction between municipalities and villages?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you do know how many municipalities there are in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head I do not recall the precise number, but I believe it's somewhere around 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you toured ten of them, ten municipalities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I could answer that question with time and reviewing my records, but I do not recall accurately the precise number. I could mention for you some of the municipalities I do remember visiting, if that's of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously Pristina; Djakovica; the Drenica region, which is actually two municipalities, Srbica and Glogovac, and I was in both; the Pec municipality; the Suva Reka municipality; Prizren municipality; I know that I visited Podujevo and Vucitrn. I'm not sure which municipalities those towns are in. And the Orahovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was mostly border municipalities, towards the border with Albania and partially with Macedonia that you visited, apart from Pristina municipality?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I spent substantial time in the Glogovac and Srbica area, and both of those are in the interior of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So we can say then that you mainly visited the border municipalities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's accurate because an important focus of our work was in Drenica, so I spent substantial time in, for example, the Gornje Obrinje village and area, which is in the Glogovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In these three instances of your three-week visits to Kosovo, who were you with? Who accompanied you on your mission?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first visit in May/June, I was alone. For the September and November visits, I was with my colleague, Peter Bouckaert. And for the fourth visit, which I apologise I'm not recalling if it was December or February, I was with another colleague, Gordana Igric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you move around with some sort of an ID, a pass? Were you issued any permit by the Yugoslav authorities or the Serbian organs of authority to enable you to freely move in the territory that you were visiting?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I recall receiving accreditation from the Serbian Ministry or perhaps it's a Secretary of Information in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And with that accreditation you could move freely around all these areas that we referred to?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accreditation was intended to allow that free movement, but at times we were blocked by government forces from obtaining access to particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In these three instances, the first time when you were on your own and the second time with your colleague and the third time with yet another colleague, how many interviews did you take and in how many places and in respect of how many incidents, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question which could be answered by referencing my records. On the first trip, where I was alone, for sure I interviewed at least 40 individuals with regards to our investigations. In the subsequent two visits with Mr. Bouckaert, that number is surely twice that, given the -- given that my colleague also conducted interviews. And in the final trip I recall doing extensive research on abuse and detention and the destruction of civilian property, which also involved extensive interviews, certainly more than two dozen. But to give you a precise number, I'm not able at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say "twice as many on the second and third visit," do you mean taking the visits together or do you mean twice as many on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Taking the visits together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I got it right now, so it is 60 interviews in all for all the three visits, right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say 60? I -- I'm not able to answer that question because I truly do not recall the precise number. If you were asking me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What I want to know you don't have to remember the exact number, of course. I would like to know whether each of these 60 alleged interviews was associated with a specific incident, or did you discuss a -- one incident with a number of people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By my calculation there's at least 144 here. 40 plus 80 plus 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. You are right, Your Honour. I lost track of the one with the colleague, but of course I was mistaken in my calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the question remains the same. Were these different incidents or were a number of people associated with a single specific incident?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These interviews were conducted in connection with a multitude of incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, we need to interrupt about now. Can you find a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps it is a suitable moment right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, just before the break we discussed the number of municipalities in Kosovo. I'm interested in the following. What if I told you that there are 29 municipalities in Kosovo instead of 14?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I would believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you carried out a very thorough research of violations of human rights in a confined area, it sounds to me as if you were not diligent enough not knowing this piece of information, since you stated that the number was 14 instead of 29.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then perhaps there is confusion on my part between the municipalities and the districts. I was referring, when I mentioned Glogovac, Srbica, Orahovac, and so on, to administrative districts. It was how we divided the province up when doing our statistical analysis, instead of to the particular municipalities, which apparently you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what if I told you in response to that that there are seven districts and not 14?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, maybe I can request to see the relevant section of Under Orders to provide you with a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There is no need for that. This suffices. I will move on to another topic. I was just trying to offer a comment about what you stated. To go back to your statement, this is P2228. Since it is actually a compilation of three different statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please in e-court see the statement dated the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can you repeat the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date, Your Honour, is the 8th until the 11th of March, 1993 -- 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third page in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you follow it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the questions without it, but perhaps for your reference and use you should have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 3 of 14. Perhaps the ERN number would be of some help. 225290. This is the page. The fourth paragraph from the top. It begins: "On the 7th of June, 1998 ..." Here you mention an incident in the village of Vasiljevo, which is the village closest to Novi Poklek. The incident you mention in this paragraph, when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident took place in the incident of Poklek, not in Vasiljevo. Vasiljevo was where the villagers had -- had fled to because Poklek was not safe at that time. The precise incident in Poklek, I do not recall the exact date, but it would have been in spring of 1998, I assume -- I believe in April or May -- actually, if I'm not mistaken, May 31st, but I would have to check to be precise, but I think it is May 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you also allow for the possibility that it was in April, significantly prior to you being in Vasiljevo.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident definitely took place prior to my arrival in Vasiljevo. When exactly it took place I would have to check the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If we go back a paragraph, the same page of the same statement, there you mention an incident in Likosane and Cirez. And you state that on the 24th of May, 1998 you were there. Do you know when the incident you discuss here took place, the incident you collected information on the 24th of May, 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The incidents in Likosane and Cirez both occurred on February 28th and March 1st of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, almost two months before you went there and had that interview, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the transcript - that was my learned friend Mr. Stamp's examination-in-chief - you stated that you came to the area of Drenica as late as September 1998 and that you carried out a detailed investigation in December. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first visit to the Drenica region was in May of 1998, specifically May 24th. I subsequently visited Drenica again in late September to conduct the investigations into the Gornje Obrinje killings that we have mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you spoke about this detailed investigation, I'm interested in the following. On the 24th of May you were there by yourself; in September you were there with another colleague by the name of Bouckaert. What did this detailed investigation encompass? Did you have any forensic experts with you, forensic pathologists, ballistic experts, and so on and so forth, or did it only encompass interviews with some people?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Mr. Bouckaert and I have extensive experience operating in war zones, and as a part of that we conduct investigations -- multi-pronged investigations. The essential element is the interview, as I've mentioned, but in addition we survey the scene, we draw a map of the environment, we look at the physical evidence to determine what took place. We do not conduct extensive forensic examinations because we do not have that expertise. In the Gornje Obrinje case, we advocated for such an investigation but it did not take place. It was blocked. A forensic team was blocked from performing its investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, in the other cases -- well, first I wanted to ask you: What is your profession? What is your degree? Which schools you attended, which universities?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a bachelor's degree in German language and international studies and a master's degree in international affairs, with a concentration in eastern Europe, media, and human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me what that has to do with any forensic science, forensic pathology, and ballistics?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have formal training in forensic science. I have never claimed to have such formal training, but I do have experience in conducting human rights investigations, both in non-conflict and conflict environments, which includes training in tasks -- I would say tasks such as overview assessments of crime scenes and determination of hostilities, determination of whether hostilities occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Fine. You've stated now and before as well that you had previous experience from war-affected areas. I'm not asking you about your experience as you -- as it is now, but as it was before 1998. What war-affected areas did you visit prior to that and what investigations did you carry out in those areas?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most relevant investigations -- well, human rights investigations were in Czech and Slovak Republics, as well as in Albania. The Albanian example does include an element of armed conflict because of the 1997 violence that took place in the fall -- in March of that year, March throughout the rest of 1997. But in terms of an armed conflict under international law, Kosovo was the first such investigation that I participated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we're discussing investigations, perhaps you can tell me something. You probably remember testifying before this Tribunal in the case against Mr. Milosevic. Is it correct that in your answer to one of Mr. Milosevic's questions, this is page 6.113 of the transcript, his question was: "Is bombing civilian targets a crime?" And there you provide an answer. Perhaps you will forgive me for my translating. You stated: "The Human Rights Watch organisation did not conclude that NATO committed war crimes, although the organisation was critical of it because of some targets hit by NATO. We didn't have compelling evidence to show that NATO intentionally targeted civilian targets." Then there was a comment by Mr. Milosevic, where he said that NATO had used cluster bombs on page 6.114. Your reply was that your organisation was critical of the use of cluster bombs because such ordnance does not distinguish between types of target and that you've expressed your concern, but nevertheless that your threshold for evidence is a very -- or the benchmark is a very high one and that it is the same for all your research and investigation. "Without a final compelling proof, we cannot establish the existence of a war crime." Is it correct, and did you indeed state this in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really have to see the precise English-language statement to comment in particular on your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the usher's assistance I can have that distributed. But I do have to say that there are some notes of ours there, some scribbling. But the essence is there and I believe it may be of help. Those are pages 6113 and 6114.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. If you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While this is happening, Mr. Bakrac, you may be able to assist me. We've got three-quarters of an hour remaining today. We will have to adjourn at quarter to 2.00. If the witness has to come back, he has to come back. But perhaps you could bear in mind that it would be a pity if he had to come back because we need an extra five minutes. And the same applies to Mr. Lukic. And it may be that the cross is going to be much longer and nothing can be done about it, but I simply draw it to your attention just in case there's a possibility of finishing his evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Please forgive me if I ask -- if I interrupt and ask you something. Whether something is a crime or not is not to be asked from a witness. We have to discern it ourselves whether something is a crime or not. And if such a statement was made in a counter-part case, that made no difference because I don't know how it -- on what basis that was accepted being a relevant question. But I'm opposing this because you cannot ask such a question from a witness, whether such-and-such thing is a crime or not. It's a legal question, and this sort of question is not asked in cross-examination. This is my respectful view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I fully understand. The point of my question is the degree and way of proving something, and through these answers we are trying to establish, if I may call it so, the double standard and double criteria used. That's why I asked the witness about the nature of the investigations he carried out. Concerning what he stated in the other case, that relates directly to the way such investigations were carried out and conclusions were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to add some points to this as well. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on with you question, please, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I resume I just wanted to provide an answer I still owe to you. I will do my best to conclude until quarter to 2.00, but even under such circumstances Mr. Lukic would not have had the time. Therefore, the witness will have to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand that may be necessary, but please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you've had sufficient time to review this. Is it correct that you actually testified to this effect? Don't you see the great discrepancy between what you said and the way you described your detailed investigations, as you call them, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this testimony is correct; but, no, I don't believe there is a discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You believe, therefore, that three visits of three weeks each and speaking to some people in a limited number of municipalities and speaking only to some people suffice to carry out an investigation and come up with a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four missions we undertook between May 1998 and March 1999 were extensive in nature. And while I am not able to provide an exact number at this moment of interviewees and municipalities visited, I can testify that they were exhaustive and extensive investigations, as was the subsequent investigation of the NATO bombing's impact on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I don't want to argue with you here. I'm interested in the following only. Did you talk to the other side or did you only get the statements from Albanian civilians? Did you try to obtain a statement concerning a given incident from the other side as well or -- and did your investigation only include taking civilian statements who -- civilians who were Albanian and photographing the sites?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We strove to document abuses on all sides and the report, Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo includes substantial information about abuses against Serbian civilians or -- as well as ethnic Albanians by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, it seems we didn't understand each other. For example, when we discuss the incident in the villages of Likosane and Cirez, by way of example, did you talk to the alleged perpetrators? Did you try to hear out the other side or did you only talk to Albanians?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cases of Likosane and Cirez, we attempted to get information by means of the letters that were sent. We also -- I personally had a meeting with Mr. Drobnjak, as mentioned, although I do not recall the conversation well enough to tell you whether we specifically discussed Likosane and Cirez. But we made efforts to obtain and present the government's view, also by citing public records and media reports that quoted government officials or gave government positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you keep saying "we." Didn't you a moment ago tell us that in May and June you were there by yourself?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. It is more appropriate for -- to say "me," personally, although working in an organisation I do have the support and consultation of a large staff. So clearly I was the responsible researcher, but I did have constant discussions with my colleagues and my directors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, further to this topic of detailed investigations, I would like to turn now to P437, page 63 in the English version. In e-court that's page 71. Do you have that before you, that part of your report? This is the report from October 1998.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that in front of me, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a different one of the statements or is this the -- are we now going into one of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour -- yes, I said that it is a report dated October 1998 and that is in the English page 63 of the document. In e-court it is page 63 of P437.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't happen to have the -- a copy of this report, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friends helped me out. It seems I do have a hard copy. With the usher's assistance, I've located the page in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think -- no, no, we're -- is that the page now on the screen, 55?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How about that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Could the witness please look at the fourth paragraph beginning with: "Also on July 11th two Mother Theresa Society activists in Djakovica ..." I apologise, Your Honour, the third paragraph beginning with: "The incident was the second reported attack on Mother Theresa activists. On July 11th, three men were fired upon by police believed to be the police while returning from an aid delivery in the village of Sibovac near Obilic. Xhevdet Stulcaku, vice-president of the Mother Theresa Society in Obilic, was struck on the head with a bullet and is currently paralyzed on the right side of his body." Is that the incident described in your statement dated the 8th until the 11th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check this statement to be sure that this refers to the statement, but I do recall this incident and I do recall interviewing Mr. Stulcaku, who was paralyzed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if you take my word for it, otherwise I can show it to you, you entered this in your statement on violations of -- of international humanitarian law. And in doing that, you thought the investigation was detailed enough because you obviously state that he was shot at by men believed to be members of the police. Do you still believe this is a sufficient degree of proving something or anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm objecting -- he's asking him to verify to the passage in the statement. And I think the witness did ask if he could see -- he did suggest that if he was shown that passage he could be more precise in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying, Mr. Bakrac, that this is specifically referred to in the statement P2228, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If you'll allow me just one minute to find it. Your Honours, that is -- that is on page 4. I assume it is page 5 of the English version of the statement that we referred to from the 8th to the 11th of March, and we are talking about the fifth paragraph "on the 22nd of September, 1998, [deleted] I talked to [deleted] who had been hit in a head by the bullet during the attack of the 11th of June." Is this the incident that you referred to? I believe that that is the incident that the book refers to also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The paragraph you may be referring to is actually the striking of a young girl, I think. It starts: "In September 1998 in Pristina hospital," is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting. In the B/C/S version it is page number 4. And in English it is the fifth page. I apologise, Your Honours, it is also page number 4 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is 4 of 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, 4 of 14, Your Honour. It begins with -- the second paragraph from the end, the next-to-penultimate paragraph. It starts with paragraph 8 of the report of Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So is this the incident that you refer to in your statement? Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, by your leave, Your Honours, read it out for the witness. At chapter 8 of the HRW, October 1998, titled "attacks and restrictions on medical and relief personnel." "I referred to a number of incidents and witnesses on 22 September. I interviewed [deleted] who was struck in the head with a bullet during the attack on 11 July, 1998 and is currently paralysed on the right side of his body. I also interviewed his physical therapist and members of his family." Is that the event?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that your detailed investigation into this incident, which you call an attack, ascertained that some people shot at this person, some people believed to be policemen?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question would require me to consult the material more in depth. My recollection is that witnesses saw the police in the area at that time, but I cannot give you precise information. I frankly just don't recall the precision -- the specific details of this case. I can certainly obtain it for you, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is it, Mr. Bakrac, that you have a copy of this with parts deleted? You omit -- or did you deliberately omit the name yourself when you were asking a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no. I have this version with struck out names right now and I was using that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you do have one which has the name in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, your conclusion is based on the fact that there was police there, some people saw that there was police there, but nobody actually saw them shooting at this person?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly do not know whether one of our witnesses said that they saw the police shooting. I would have to consult the material directly to give you an exact answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. During a certain period in 1998 you also spent time in the northern parts of Albania, right?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What period was that?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in July -- perhaps it was June, late June/early July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you were staying in north Albania, did you happen to see any KLA training camps?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training camps I did not see, but I did encounter individuals from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when you say that you encountered individuals, did you have such encounters in their headquarters or were these just chance encounters?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One encounter I recall was in the hotel of Bajram Curri, where we met a man who said he was a commander, and I do not recall his name. Many people claimed to be commanders when they were not. I also recall the -- the KLA had captured two soldiers or men who claimed to be soldiers. They had deserted from the army, so they claimed, and the KLA held a kind of press conference, if you could, to present these men. And these men gave a public statement and were then handed over to the OSCE, which was also present in northern Albania at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We shall come to that detail very quickly. But before that could you tell me, please, whether these persons from the KLA wore uniforms, what kind of weapons did they have, what kinds of uniforms they wore, if they had uniforms on and such details, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The individual in the hotel was not wearing uniform, nor was he armed, or perhaps he had a concealed weapon. The individuals who held this so-called press conference I do not recall, but I do believe they were in uniform. I did not recall the weapons that they have. They were certainly not openly visible; in other words, the KLA obviously -- they considered this territory secure, so there were not armed guards in defensive positions. But there may have been weapons in their -- in the -- in their presence. If anything, they would have been automatic rifles, probably AK-47.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, please be so kind as to tell me what uniforms do they wear? Were those uniforms of the Albanian army or some other uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, but I know I subsequently saw in Kosovo and probably -- but I'm not certain if I saw them in northern Albania, although I know they were certainly in northern Albania, KLA members who were in what I would military uniform, green, but distinctly with insignia of the KLA; in particular, it says "UCK," which is the Albanian acronym for Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Bajram Curri is in the territory of the Republic of Albania, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, now we should go back to what you said a while ago, namely in this place Bajram Curri at a press conference you saw two soldiers and Montenegrins, you say in your statement, Montenegrins who had deserted the Yugoslav army. First of all, I should like to ask you whether you talked to them and interviewed them.
