utterances.speaker: FREDERICK ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke to them very briefly, but we did not conduct an interview with them. And the reason is that we were not confident about the independence of their statements. Given the fact they were in KLA custody, we were not certain whether these individuals would feel free to give us independent and objective information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm very happy with your reply, and more so that's why I'm all the more surprised why the allegations about the statements of these two soldiers actually formed part of your statement because right now you said that you did not conduct an interview with them because it was obviously impossible for them to give you detailed and true information under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. That is not a question. That is a comment from counsel. But again, I would ask just to refer us to the point, if it's not too difficult, in the statement that is being cited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you direct your attention, please, Mr. Bakrac, to the part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a minute to find it. That is the same statement from the 8th to the 11th of March, 1999, page 8 of 14, paragraph the fifth from the top. It starts "on the 21st of June, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In fact, you quote their words which they uttered at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you will allow me to respond, I'm not eliciting a comment. The witness has just said that he did not conduct an interview with them because he was doubtful as to the objectivity and validity of such an interview, in view of the fact that they were in custody and have been imprisoned by the Albanians. So it is my question rather than a comment, the witness having said that to us now, why is this a part of his statement in the form that it is a part of it [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We presented that information -- their words, but also making clear the context in which those statements were made so the reader can deduce and decide how much weight to place on those comments. And I would ask the Court to make the section of that report available to me so that I could respond with more precision whether we had any editorial comment or placed the quotations from these alleged soldiers in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's P2228. I don't know what the number of the page is, though, for e-court. It's 8 of 14 on the statement, and it's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry, it's page 35 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the exhibit, though, that the counsel is referring to, if I may clear it up --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- 2228. And that is not the exhibit that's on the screen now. So we need page 35 of P2228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Scroll down. It's the next paragraph that we can't see. Now, right down to the bit in italics, which is the bit that counsel is interested in. That's fine. Thank you. Now, there you have the complete context, Mr. Abrahams, but bear in mind when you answer that this is your statement to the Court, it's not a report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not sure, Your Honour, if we included any of this information in the report itself. In fact, I doubt that we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate that. The question you're being asked, though, is why did you just present the matter in this way without commenting, as you have in your evidence orally, that you wouldn't rely on this evidence because of the circumstances in which it was obtained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I presented this information in order that it could be known what I had observed and -- well, frankly, with retrospect I would add the qualifying paragraph that I expressed here today; namely, that we did not conduct an in-depth investigation -- interview with these gentlemen because of our concerns about their reliability as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it -- because we are near our break I will ask a question which I consider to be of the essence, and I want to ask it before the break. This is also this statement from the 8th to the 11th of March, 1999. In English the page number is 10 of 14, the third paragraph. In e-court it is page 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the court reporter can't hear you because the interpreter's microphone is still on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. All I was saying is that this gives us the answer to another question that was asked earlier which is the number of times that Mr. Abrahams visited Kosovo during the relevant period, and this statement was the one produced in much nearer -- produced much nearer to the time and indicates five visits. Please carry on, Mr. Bakrac, with your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, turn his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to read a part of the statement of this witness, and I shall ask him to give me an answer on the basis of what we have been discussing so far about the number of his visits, who he was accompanied by on these visits, and the sentence is as follows. "From May 1998 until February 1999, I witnessed a pattern of destruction throughout the villages in Kosovo which had been caused by offences by Serbian forces through five separate missions to Kosovo." So the question now is: Is it three or four, or is it four or five? And can the witness make such an allegation, given what we have heard from him about the situation in the territory, how -- how they were able to cover the territory in terms of their staff and in view of the fact that he was there with just a colleague, one colleague of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions there, Mr. Abrahams: How many times you visited; and can you make this assertion based on the visits that you paid? And when you've completed the answer to that, then we'll be adjourning. So could you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I do rely on my sworn statement that it was five missions. Perhaps there was some confusion over whether I was referring to only the visits in 1998, but there definitely was a final visit in early 1999 I recall precisely because it was just in the days prior to the first Rambouillet negotiations. So I certainly was there in 1999 and four times then in 1998. As to our coverage of the conflict at that time, I personally undertook those five missions. My colleague, Peter Bouckaert, was with me on two of them. We also had a third individual, Gordana Igric, who was repeatedly frequently in the province. She lived in Belgrade, travelled to Kosovo frequently. I'm distinctly aware of two research missions she undertook there. In February 1999 I was together with her. And if my memory serves me correctly, also in December 1998 I was with her. And there may be other times as well when she was in Kosovo. So those three researchers, myself and two others, were the people who conducted the research on which our conclusions are based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were your investigations sufficient to reach the conclusions that you've set out in the paragraph -- or at least to make the statement, rather, not the conclusion, but the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that we conducted adequate investigations to reach the conclusions, as published in our reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will have to adjourn there for today. I'm afraid, Mr. Abrahams, that means that you have to come back here, and that will be on the 7th of August for a 9.00 start. Meanwhile, I don't think I need to remind you, but I think it's only right that I should so everyone hears the position clearly being acknowledged by you, that between now and then you should have no communication with anyone at all about the evidence you've given or the evidence you're about to give in the case. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, the court is now adjourned until the 7th of August at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
